# A Global Approach to the Theory of Special Finsler Manifolds

## Overview and Objectives

The primary aim of this paper is to develop a global, coordinate-free presentation of the theory of special Finsler manifolds. Traditional treatments of Finsler geometry have often relied heavily on local coordinate computations, which, while computationally accessible, can obscure the underlying geometric structures and their invariant properties. By adopting an intrinsic, coordinate-free framework, this work seeks to illuminate the fundamental geometric nature of special Finsler manifolds and to provide a more unified and conceptually transparent foundation for their study.

## Intrinsic Definitions of Special Finsler Manifolds

A central contribution of this paper is the introduction and systematic investigation of intrinsic definitions for many of the most important and commonly used classes of special Finsler manifolds. Among the types considered are Berwald manifolds, Landsberg manifolds, and a variety of manifolds characterized by specific curvature conditions and recurrence properties. By formulating these definitions in a global, coordinate-free manner, the paper establishes precise geometric characterizations that are independent of any particular choice of local coordinates, thereby clarifying the essential features that distinguish each class.

## Relationships Among Special Finsler Manifolds

Beyond providing intrinsic definitions, the paper establishes numerous relationships between the different types of special Finsler manifolds under consideration. These interconnections reveal how the various classes relate to one another, identifying implications, inclusions, and equivalences among them. Such a network of relationships not only deepens the theoretical understanding of these manifolds but also serves as a valuable reference for further investigations in the field.

## Global Results and New Contributions

An important feature of this work is that many results previously known only in a local setting are here proved globally. This transition from local to global reasoning strengthens the theoretical foundation and demonstrates the coordinate-independent validity of these results. In addition, the paper obtains several entirely new results, expanding the existing body of knowledge in the theory of special Finsler manifolds. The investigation is further supported by the derivation of a number of useful identities concerning the torsion and curvature tensor fields, which play a crucial role throughout the analysis and are likely to prove valuable in subsequent research.

## Appendix: Local Counterpart for Comparison

To complement the global treatment and to facilitate comparison, the paper includes an appendix presenting the local counterpart of the global approach. This appendix allows readers to relate the intrinsic, coordinate-free formulations developed in the main text to their more familiar local coordinate expressions. By providing this bridge between the two perspectives, the appendix enhances the accessibility of the work and underscores the consistency between the global and local formulations of the theory.

# A Global Theory of Special Finsler Manifolds

## Introduction and Motivation

Finsler geometry, as a natural generalization of Riemannian geometry, has long attracted attention for its capacity to describe geometric structures in which the metric depends not only on position but also on direction. Within this rich framework, certain distinguished classes of Finsler manifolds—characterized by special properties of their connection, curvature, or torsion tensors—occupy a central role. These "special Finsler manifolds" include, among others, locally Minkowskian spaces, Berwald manifolds, Landsberg manifolds, and a variety of spaces defined through curvature conditions or recurrence relations. Historically, however, much of the theory surrounding these classes has been developed within a local coordinate framework, which, while computationally accessible, tends to obscure the underlying geometric structure and often restricts results to local statements.

This paper undertakes the task of building a **global, coordinate-free (intrinsic) theory** of special Finsler manifolds. The motivation is twofold: first, to place the study of these important spaces on a firm invariant foundation that reflects their intrinsic geometric nature; and second, to strengthen and extend the existing body of results by lifting them from the local to the global setting.

## The Intrinsic Approach

The cornerstone of our development is the systematic introduction of **intrinsic definitions** for each of the special classes under consideration. Rather than characterizing a Berwald or Landsberg manifold through the behavior of connection coefficients in local charts, we formulate their defining properties in terms of globally defined geometric objects—vector fields, torsion tensors, and curvature tensors on the pullback bundle—that carry no reference to a particular coordinate system. This intrinsic formulation not only clarifies the essential features distinguishing one class from another but also renders the interrelations among them transparent.

Working within this framework, we examine in detail the **relationships and hierarchies** among the numerous types of special Finsler manifolds. We investigate, for instance, the precise conditions under which a Landsberg manifold reduces to a Berwald manifold, how locally Minkowskian spaces sit within the broader landscape of flat and curvature-restricted manifolds, and the logical implications connecting recurrence-based classes to those defined by curvature properties. The resulting network of implications provides a unified map of the terrain, organizing what has often appeared as a collection of loosely related definitions into a coherent structural picture.

## Principal Results

The intrinsic and global character of our methods yields several kinds of results:

- **Globalization of local theorems.** Many classical results, previously established only in local coordinates, are shown to hold globally. By reformulating the hypotheses and conclusions in coordinate-free terms, we demonstrate that these theorems reflect genuinely global geometric phenomena rather than artifacts of a chosen chart.

- **New results.** Beyond recovering known statements, the intrinsic viewpoint enables us to prove entirely new theorems concerning the classification and characterization of special Finsler manifolds, several of which do not arise naturally—or at all—within the local formalism.

- **Useful identities.** Along the way, we derive a number of **identities for the torsion and curvature tensor fields**. These identities are of independent interest, serving both as essential tools in our proofs and as convenient formulas for future investigations in Finsler geometry.

## Significance

Taken together, these developments furnish a **unified intrinsic framework** for the study of special Finsler manifolds. By dispensing with coordinate dependence and emphasizing global geometric structure, the theory advances our understanding of these spaces in a way that is both conceptually clarifying and technically powerful. It consolidates disparate strands of the existing literature, extends the reach of established results, and opens avenues for further inquiry into the geometry of Finsler manifolds and their many important special classes.

# The Finsler and Minkowskian Geometries

Finsler geometry represents one of the most elegant generalizations of Riemannian geometry, extending the classical notions of distance and length in profound ways. At its heart lies the study of spaces where the concept of length depends not only on position but also on direction, offering a richer framework for understanding the geometry of manifolds.

## The Foundations of Finsler Geometry

The Finsler structure on a manifold is defined by a function that measures the length of tangent vectors. Unlike Riemannian geometry, where this length arises from an inner product, Finsler geometry permits a more general norm. This function must satisfy certain conditions—positivity, homogeneity, and convexity—yet it need not derive from a quadratic form. This subtle distinction opens the door to an entire universe of geometric possibilities that Riemannian geometry cannot capture.

The name honors Paul Finsler, whose 1918 doctoral thesis systematized these ideas, though the foundational concepts trace back to Bernhard Riemann himself, who had already glimpsed the possibility of such generalizations in his famous inaugural lecture of 1854.

## The Minkowskian Connection

The Minkowskian geometry occupies a special place within this broader theory. A Minkowski space is essentially the simplest nontrivial example of a Finsler manifold—one that is flat and translation-invariant, where the norm remains constant across all points of the space. In this sense, the Minkowskian structure serves as the local model for general Finsler geometry, much as Euclidean space serves as the model for Riemannian manifolds.

The Minkowskian framework, named after Hermann Minkowski, found its most celebrated application in the mathematical formulation of special relativity. Here, the geometry of spacetime is governed by a metric that treats time and space on unified yet distinct footing, giving rise to the light cones and causal structures that define modern physics.

## The Interplay of Ideas

What makes the relationship between the Finsler and the Minkowskian so compelling is the way local and global properties intertwine. A Finsler manifold can be understood, at each point, through its Minkowskian tangent space. The variation of these Minkowskian norms from point to point encodes the curvature and rich geometric behavior of the whole manifold.

This perspective has proven invaluable across disciplines—from theoretical physics and optics to biology and information theory—wherever anisotropic phenomena, where properties differ by direction, demand a mathematical language beyond the isotropic assumptions of classical geometry.

## Conclusion

The Finsler and Minkowskian geometries together illustrate the enduring power of mathematical generalization. By relaxing the constraints of the familiar, they reveal structures of surprising beauty and utility, continuing to inspire research at the frontiers of both pure mathematics and its applications to the physical world.

Working on the pullback bundle over the slit tangent bundle, we characterize several important classes of Finsler spaces—including Riemannian, locally Minkowskian, Berwald, Landsberg, and $C$-reducible manifolds, as well as spaces of scalar and constant flag curvature—through intrinsic tensorial conditions expressed in terms of the fundamental geometric objects: the Barthel connection, the Cartan, Berwald, Chern-Rund, and Hashiguchi connections, and their associated curvature and torsion tensors.

We establish the mutual relationships and hierarchical structure among these special Finsler manifolds, deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for a given Finsler space to belong to each class. Particular attention is devoted to the intrinsic characterization of the Cartan torsion tensor $\mathbf{T}$, the mean Cartan torsion, and the Landsberg tensor, whose vanishing or degeneracy governs the transition between distinct geometric categories. We further clarify the interrelations between the vanishing of the $h$- and $v$-curvature tensors of the various canonical connections and the classification of the underlying manifold.

The coordinate-free treatment not only illuminates the geometric meaning of classical results, freeing them from computational artifacts of local coordinates, but also reveals structural relationships that are obscured in the index notation. Several classical theorems, including intrinsic versions of the Deicke, Numata, and Szabó theorems, are recovered and extended within this unified framework. The results contribute to a coherent global theory of Finsler geometry and provide a foundation for further investigation of the interplay between the intrinsic curvature structure and the special properties of Finsler manifolds.

# Abstract

**A Coordinate-Free Study of Special Finsler Manifolds**

We present a global, coordinate-free investigation of several classes of special Finsler manifolds, developing an intrinsic framework based on the pullback bundle formalism and the associated Berwald and Cartan connections. Working entirely on the pullback of the tangent bundle over the slit tangent bundle, we characterize each special class through invariant tensorial conditions imposed on the fundamental linear connections, thereby avoiding any dependence on local coordinate expressions.

Within this framework, we treat the classes of Riemannian, locally Minkowskian, Berwald, Landsberg, general Landsberg, $C$-reducible, $C_2$-like, $S_3$-like, $S_4$-like, quasi-$C$-reducible, semi-$C$-reducible, $P$-reducible, $P^*$-Finsler, and $h$-isotropic manifolds. For each class we provide a purely intrinsic definition and derive its principal properties. In total, **twenty-two known local results**—previously established only through local computations in a fixed coordinate system—are here proved globally in a coordinate-free manner, clarifying their invariant geometric content and interrelations.

In addition, we obtain **several new global results**. Among these, we establish new intrinsic characterizations relating the vanishing of certain torsion and curvature tensors to membership in the above classes, prove global equivalences among the reducibility conditions under suitable dimensional hypotheses, and derive necessary and sufficient conditions—expressed through the $v$-covariant derivative of the Cartan torsion and the mixed curvature—for a general Landsberg manifold to reduce to a Berwald manifold. We further clarify the precise logical implications among the special classes, correcting and completing certain inclusions that were previously stated only locally.

An **appendix** is devoted to a systematic comparison between the global (coordinate-free) definitions introduced here and their classical local counterparts. For each special class we explicitly recover the traditional local formulation from the intrinsic one, verifying their equivalence and demonstrating that the present global formulation faithfully generalizes—and in some cases sharpens—the existing local theory.

---

**Keywords:** Finsler manifold, pullback bundle, Cartan connection, Berwald connection, Landsberg manifold, $C$-reducible, coordinate-free geometry.

**MSC 2020:** 53C60, 53B40, 58B20.
